There are many things I like about the Scrum methodology.

I like that it’s difficult to hide and go unnoticed. I prefer people who expose themselves, take risks, and accept the consequences. It’s tempting to hide behind the curtain, but it’s much more exciting to step out and be on stage.

I like being able to do retrospectives at the end and having the opportunity to improve, to criticize and receive criticism, to grow and become stronger.

I like that it doesn’t matter who does what or how long it takes to do something. What matters is that the work gets done. What’s the point of the rest if not to create reproaches and bad feelings? Out with it, I’m not interested.

But of all the good things it has, what I like most is finishing a sprint and starting another. I haven’t seen a moment when the team is more focused, motivated, and excited. Because it’s an opportunity to (this time) do things right. Tabula rasa, we start anew, good luck and good sprint.

The atmosphere is fantastic, the team breathes optimism and excitement. And without realizing it (at least in my case) that spirit of renewal seeps into my general behavior, into my daily life. How useful it is to set a goal and the different steps to achieve it. To set a milestone and a date, achieve it or not, modify it, adapt it, improve it, and start again.

It’s the carrot at the end of the stick that helps me move forward. It’s true that as you get closer to the carrot, it looks more wilted and unappetizing. With each step, you encounter difficulties, stumble, it moves away, it dangles grudgingly, and often when you’re really close, almost touching it, you see that the carrot wasn’t much to begin with.

But it doesn’t matter because when you get there (if you get there), you take a couple of half-hearted bites, toss it, and build a new, longer stick to place a new and shiny carrot. A thousand times more appetizing than the previous one, with a much smoother stick, with impeccable conditions, nothing like before, to achieve your goal. Because what’s important is not the carrot itself, it’s just a star to hitch your wagon to, and there are infinite stars. It’s the journey that enriches you.

Let’s never underestimate the power of making a “check” (or “done”). People love it, I love it. There’s immense power in it. That’s why I like to set realistic and small goals and achieve them. That little daily victory, that boost of self-esteem. It’s the ultimate moral doping.

It’s one of the practices that have helped me most in my daily life. Let’s say, for example, I aim to not use the elevator at least two days a week. Come on, who can’t achieve that? It’s a mini-goal, any kid runs up and down the stairs thinking about what awaits at the end of them, without even noticing if there are three or a hundred steps. Anyone can do that.

Then Sunday comes, and I’ve achieved one of the goals... it feels good. If you add the rest and have enough consistency and discipline, nothing can stop you.

You have to be reasonable... nobody is infallible, and sometimes we allow ourselves some leeway, we don’t reach everything. It’s part of the game, an indispensable part even. If we always achieved everything, we’d lose the spark. It would be like always winning a bet, not much fun.

I encourage myself to continue with my practices, to propose new, healthier habits, to insist and incorporate them into my routine. I declare myself addicted to the comforting feeling that comes with it. I like to look at myself in the mirror before going to sleep and not only not be ashamed of what I see but feel proud of what I’ve achieved (and what’s yet to come).
